NO. 045 · Hunters of the Sky / Falconidae · Falcons

Common Kestrel

红隼 · hóng sǔn Falco tinnunculus
Winter visitor / resident Common 32–38 cm Protected (Class II) IUCN LC

The small raptor that can stop in mid-air

It has a trick most raptors cannot manage: hovering into the wind with its head held perfectly still, staring at the ground for mice, then dropping vertically. That is the classic picture of a Kestrel.

Gallery

One scientific illustration for shape and colour blocks, two field photographs for how it looks in real light. Click any image to enlarge.

Identification

  • MaleCrown and tail blue-grey, back chestnut with black spots, a broad black band near the tip of the tail.
  • FemaleBrown throughout, the back densely barred dark, the tail with several bars — altogether plainer than the male.
  • FaceThe dark moustachial stripe typical of falcons, running down from the eye, with conspicuous yellow bare skin around it.
  • FlightWings pointed and long with rapid beats; when hovering the wings vibrate at high frequency while the tail is fanned for balance.

Behaviour

A skilled hoverer, but it also perches on poles, streetlights and the edges of tall buildings to wait. It feeds mainly on rodents and large insects, and takes small birds and lizards. South China has both residents and winter visitors; it is seen over city high-rises as well as farmland. It nests in gaps in buildings and in tree holes, and builds no nest of its own.

Voice

A sharp, rapid 'kii-kii-kii' or 'kee-kee-kee', a high chattering series, usually near the nest or when alarmed.

Where to find it in Zhuhai

  • Doumen farmland power lines
  • city rooftop ledges
  • Jinwan grassy slopes
  • Hengqin open ground
Field note
A nationally protected species (Class II). A small raptor hanging motionless in the air is almost certainly a Kestrel — the trick is its trademark.
